extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American political history and constitutional law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and analyze the nature, institutions, powers, and limits of American State governments and their constitutions, as presented in a political science / constitutional law textbook chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each State makes its own Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State makes its own Constitution; the people agree on their form of government for themselves with no interference from other States or from the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form is subject to one condition only: it must be republican. Newer States tended to copy older States' constitutions; constitutional language, outlines and phrases reappear across States (e.g., precedents set by Virginia influenced Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Florida).

rubrics_metrics.name: State institutions (core list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State has its own: Constitution; Executive (governor and various officials); Legislature of two Houses; system of local government in counties, cities, townships, and school districts; system of State and local taxation; debts; body of private law; system of civil and criminal procedure; a court from which no appeal lies (except in certain federal matters); and a scheme of citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter lists these as the principal components by which a State's legal independence and right of self-government appears. Each item is explained elsewhere in the text and together they cover nearly all ordinary relations of citizens to one another and to government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional supremacy within the State
rubrics_metrics.description: The government of each State is determined by and set forth in its Constitution, a comprehensive fundamental law enacted by the people of the State and capable of being repealed or altered only by the people themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A State Constitution stands above the State legislature; any statute inconsistent with it is invalid. The Constitution is a 'rigid' or 'supreme' instrument: a frame of government established by a superior authority creating a subordinate law-making body limited by the instrument's terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral legislature (typical structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State typically has a Legislature of two Houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a standard institutional attribute of State governments; the bicameral form is presented as the usual design for State legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive authority (governor and officials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State has an Executive consisting of a governor and various other officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executive is one of the core State institutions; its composition and powers vary by State but are part of the independent State governmental structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local government as creature of the State
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of a State over all communities within its limits is absolute; it may grant or refuse local government as it pleases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a State might extinguish a municipality and govern the city by a State-appointed commissioner; local governments have no right of complaint to the Federal government against such State measures. Cities are legally subordinate to the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and local taxation system
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State establishes its own system of State and local taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-collected direct taxes and taxes administered under State law are the routine means by which citizens fund State/local services; taxation is enumerated among the State's distinctive powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State debts and repudiation power
rubrics_metrics.description: States have debts which they may repudiate at their own pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter lists repudiation of debt as an attribute a State may possess; this illustrates the breadth of State autonomy over financial obligations (subject to political and legal constraints discussed elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of private law under State control
rubrics_metrics.description: The State controls a body of private law, including the whole law of real and personal property, of contracts, of torts, of crimes, and of family relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These substantive areas affecting day-to-day relations among citizens are primarily State law domains; they demonstrate how States cover most ordinary relations between citizens and their government.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of procedure (civil and criminal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State has its own system of procedure, civil and criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural law (how courts operate, trial processes, appeals within State courts) is a State competency and part of its institutional independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: State court finality except in federal matters
rubrics_metrics.description: States have courts 'from which no appeal lies (except in cases touching Federal legislation or the Federal constitution) to any Federal court.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State courts are final in matters of State law; only cases involving federal questions may be appealed to federal courts. This delineates the judicial boundary between State and Federal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: State citizenship and its variations
rubrics_metrics.description: State citizenship may admit persons (for example, recent immigrants) to certain privileges of citizens at times, or on conditions, wholly different from those prescribed by other States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizenship rules vary by State; active participation in Federal government (voting in congressional and presidential elections) flows from being a voting citizen of a particular State. The fourteenth and fifteenth Amendments constrain State action regarding privileges of citizenship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active US citizenship depends on State voting status
rubrics_metrics.description: A man gains active citizenship of the United States only by becoming a voting citizen of some particular State; voting power in the State carries voting power in Federal elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may vary in how they grant the franchise (e.g., to recent foreigners or persons convicted of crimes); federal constitutional amendments (14th, 15th) limit state restrictions designed to protect certain groups (e.g., freedmen). Naturalization and State electoral franchises interact (naturalization makes one a citizen of both the United States and of the admitting State, but the electoral franchise depends on State laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalization: federal uniform rule and residency requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has power to pass a uniform rule of naturalization; under the laws described, a foreigner must have resided in the United States five years and one year in the State where he seeks admission, declare intent two years prior, and take an oath of renunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalization confers US and State citizenship but does not necessarily confer the electoral franchise (that depends on State law). The text gives concrete procedural requirements as an example of federal authority over naturalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population mobility and lack of natural geographic demarcation reduce State distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: No natural lines of demarcation exist for many States; constant movement of population (settlers coming from other States and continuing westward) tends to prevent the growth of local distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newer States often copied older States' constitutions and institutions; in the West, States are likened to a chain of lakes mixed by moving populations. Local peculiarities either do not develop readily or disappear as areas fill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport and communication foster national homogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Railway communication, newspapers, and the telegraph bind States together, making inhabitants across States aware of events everywhere and tending to homogenize political life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trunk lines, market dependence on Atlantic cities and Europe, leading newspapers read over a vast area. These factors tighten ties among States and reduce local distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: National political parties restrain local divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Political parties are largely the same in all States — their tenets, methods, and leaders (with some exceptions) — so State politics are swayed by forces common to the whole country, restraining growth of local parties and issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prominent man may enjoy special influence in his own State, but party organization and ideology operate across State lines, reducing local political divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption in favor of State powers (inherent authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: A State's authority is inherent, not delegated; it has all powers any independent government can have except those it can be shown to have stripped itself of, while the Federal Government has only powers affirmatively shown to have been received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal expression: 'the presumption is always for a State, and the burden of proof lies upon any one who denies its authority in a particular matter.' Historical context: this doctrine animated much debate from 1789 to 1870.

rubrics_metrics.name: State may command allegiance and punish treason
rubrics_metrics.description: A State commands the allegiance of its citizens and may punish them for treason against it; treason against a State is legally possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although rarely exercised, the legal existence of this power contributed to the Southern states' belief in the primacy of State authority during secession. Since the Civil War, allegiance to the State is subordinate to allegiance to the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on State rights after the Civil War
rubrics_metrics.description: State rights now exclude: (1) the right of secession (admitted since the war to be no longer claimable), (2) powers which the Constitution withholds from the States (e.g., intercourse with foreign governments), and (3) powers which the Constitution expressly confers on the Federal Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As to some federal-conferred powers, States may act concurrently or in default of Federal action; contravention of federal action is to be resolved by courts, ultimately by Federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between legal sovereignty and practical predominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish legal sovereignty (where law vests supreme authority) from practical predominance (the actual force able to enforce authority); legal and actual sovereignty may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benthamite confusion mixed sovereignty de jure with sovereignty de facto. The text recommends recognizing where legal claims had become incompatible with historical/national realities; 'where physical force resided' mattered in resolving conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid/supreme constitution characteristic (historic development)
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions historically grew out of colonial charters and trading-company instruments; a defining characteristic is a rigid or supreme Constitution that sets a frame of government and restricts subordinate law-making bodies from violating the instrument's terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Massachusetts charters (1628, 1691) and the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut are cited. When the connection with Britain was severed, authority over the frame passed to the people of the State, speaking through the State Constitution.
